subtopic: EXTENSION OF THE TERM OF PARLIAMENT.
subsubtopic: MOTION OF SIR ROBERT BORDEN POSTPONED.
speechtext:
Resolved, that an humble Address be presented to His Most Excellent Majesty the King, in the following words:-
To the King's Most Excellent Majesty:
Most Gracious Sovereign:
We, Your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal subjects, the	Commons of Canada,

in Parliament assembled, humbly approach Your Majesty praying that you may graciously be pleased to give your consent to submit a measure to the Parliament of the United Kingdom, to amend the British North American Act, 1867, in the manner following, or to the following effect:
"An Act to amend the British North America Act, 1867."
Be it enacted by the King's Most Excellent Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Lords, Spiritual and Temporal, and Commons, in this present Parliament assembled, and by the authority of the same, as follows:-
1.	Notwithstanding anything in the British North America Act, 1867, or In any Act amending the same, or in any Order in Council, or terms or conditions of Union, made or approved under the said Act, or under any Act of the Canadian Parliament, the term of the Twelfth Parliament of Canada is hereby extended until the seventh day of October, 1918.
2.	This Act may be cited as the British North America Act, 1917, and the British North America Act, 1867 to 1916, and this Act may be cited together as the British North America Act, 1867 to 1917.
All of which we humbly pray Your Majesty to take into your favourable and gracious consideration.

speechtext: May I be allowed to say that, while I am ready to go on-my opinion is made up and I do not think any delay will change it-still, when an hon. gentleman of the importance of my friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) makes such a request of the Government, I am very glad that the Prime Minister agrees to it. I wish to say that this is a free Parliament, and every member is free to express his opinion.

The House in Committee on Bill No. 13, to consolidate and1 amend the Railway Act. -Hon. Frank Cochrane-Mr. Blain in the Chair.
On section 5-to what persons, companies and railways applicable:

The Drayton-Acworth report, if I remember correctly, recommends that Government railways be placed under, the supervision of the Board of Railway Commissioners. That means that if the larger scheme of railway organization and control is undertaken by the Government, the Government railways will be subject to

the jurisdiction of that board. If in this Act, however, no special provision is made in that respect, the Government railways will not come under the control of the Board of Bailway Commissioners.

It is our intention to introduce am amendment to the Government Railways Act to put Government railways under the control of the Railway Commission. I expected' that the Bill would he drawn before this, but my law clerk has been ill.

Will not such an Act
conflict with this Act as it now stands?

No, we are providing
that .it will not.

I am not now expressing any opinion as to the advisability of placing the Government railways under the control of the Board of Railway Commissioners. But we are now passing an Act which provides that Government railways shall not be subject to the jurisdiction of that board. The minister says that later he will introduce an amendment to the Government Railways Act providing that Government railways shall be subject to that board. Should not the words "other than Government railways" be left out of section 5, if a Bill is to be introduced to put the Government railways under the Railway Act?
We will let the section stand until the other Bill is introduced.

In the first place, by the proposed amendment the Railway Act itself would1 be made applicable to the Government railways, and by an amendment to the Government Railways Act the latter would come under the Board of Railway Commissioners. To make the matter clear, both Acts should be amended. I agree with the proposal of the minister to let the section stand.
Section stands.
On section 6-Application to railways controlled or operated by Dominion companies.

The change is merely a reconstruction. The new words are:
Without limiting the effect of the last preceding section, extend and-
Then, on the 13th line, in paragraph (b), the word " every " is added. The whole of paragraph (c) i-s reconstructed in the present Bill.

If a provincial company with a provincial charter were to be leased to a company with a Dominion charter, the former road, notwithstanding the fact that it was a provincial railway, would come under the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada.
Yes.

This also brings up a pretty large question, namely, the joint control of railways operated between the United States and Canada. At one time a proposition was made by the Interstate Commerce Commission, and approved, partially at least, by the late Mr. Justice Mabee, w'ho was at that time chairman of the Canadian Board, that a joint board be formed of representatives from each of these boards, and that all international traffic be entrusted to this joint board. Several hearings were had before the then Minister of Railways as to the advisability of this, and while on a superficial investigation, the matter looked as if it could be worked out quite readily, when we came to the details, there were certain details with regard to the United States railways, particularly in the West, that were not wholly applicable to the Canadian railways. The head of the Railway Department at that time was convinced that the matter was one on which slow progress ought to be made, because there were many pitfalls that we did not see at first. Has the minister considered the possibility of having a board of that kind that would be governed by regulations that would be international and at the same time equitable to. the Canadian railways?

The matter has not
been brought up in my time and I have not paid very much attention to it, but if the proposition could be worked out in a satisfactory way, it would be very desirable. As the hon. member says, it is a matter on which we would have to go slow.
Section 6 agreed to.
On section 7-railroads declared to be for the general advantage of Canada.

Section 6, as I understand it, brings roads with a provincial charter under the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners, even if they are not declared to be for the general advantage of Canada, while section 7 brings such railways under the jurisdiction of that board by declaring them to be for the general advantage of Canada.
Is it not better to have them under the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners?
Most decidedly.

Section agreed to.
On section 8-Provincial railways connecting with or crossing Dominion railways.
Is this section new?

The change in this section is to bring it into conformity with the decision in Privy Council vs. The Montreal Street Railway. The words " Street Railways and Tramway " have been taken out in view of the definition of the word " railway."
That was a celebrated case.

I do not think this section differs from the old one to any great extent. I find that the changes that were in the draft Bill have all been struck out and the section is left almost exactly as it was in the old Act. I do not think there is any objection to it
Section agreed to
On section 11-Powers of Deputy Chief Commissioner.

Subsection 4, of section 11, is an addition, or amendment to, the original Act, and it is the same as it was in the draft Bill. I think the idea was that, in case of multiplicity of business, they would be able to divide the board, and ,sit in two or three places at the same time, if necessary, in order to expedite business.

Section agreed to.
On section 23-Duties of secretary.

The only change in section 23 is that in the 25th line the words " chief commissioner " are struck out, and in the 27th line, between the words " board " and " sealed," the words " duly signed and " are inserted.

That means that the
secretary shall obey the directions of the board, as well as the directions of the commissioner. It increases the power of the Chief Commissioner, to a great extent.

Is there any provision as to what will occur if the board arrive at a different conclusion from that
[sMr. Graham. ]
arrived at by the Chief Commissioner? There might be a conflict, and we should insert a section to provide for that.

I do not remember the explanation given to the commmittee as to -the change. There might be a conflict of authority there. These changes were suggested very largely by a gentleman representing the railway board at the sittings of the committee. This amendment was inserted at his request.
I think we had better let this section stand.

Very well.
Section stands.
On section 31-Annual report to Governor in Council.

In the 2nd and
4th lines the word " March " is struck out, and the word " December " inserted.

That change was
made at the request of the railways; it corresponds with the American practice. Section agreed to.
On section 33-jurisdiction:

The words
under this Act or otherwise for carrying this Act into effect ", in the twentieth line, are struck out. Then in the twenty-eighth line the words " conferred by this Act " are struck out. The last five lines in the clause are new:
And wherever by reason of insolvency, sale under mortgage, or any other cause, a railway or section thereof is operated, managed or held otherwise than by the Company, the Board may make any order it deems proper for adapting and applying the provisions of this Act to such case.

It means that in case
a railway is handed over to a receiver, the receiver is under the jurisdiction of the bo-ard. It only extends the powers of the board to cover the receiver.

That is the
idea. Under the general scheme of this Act, the Board of Railway Commissioners *is dealing with a railway company. If the company is handed over to a receiver the question arises whether, as a matter of law it does not cease to be a railway *company as a technical entity. It was therefore thought advisable to give the Board of Railway Commissioners jurisdiction over the receiver.

Section agreed to.

On section 34-power to make orders and regulations:

The statement made by Mr. Price in regard to clause 34 to 44 is that they are as to the power of the hoard to make orders and regulations. Subsections 2 and 3 of clause 34 are made more complete in order to obviate any question being raised as to the powers of the board to make orders.
iMr. GRAHAM: It would strike me that provision is made in this Act to cover any of the provisions in any other Act that might be passed.

That is what it says.
Mr. CA'RVELL:	If there is an imposition or a penalty of any kind provided by any other Act, the Board of Railway Commissioners has jurisdiction to enforce it. It practically gives the board power over all legislation governing railways, whether included in this Act or in a special Act.

Where is there
in the Act providing for its enforcement?

That is provided for
later on; there is a section regarding penalties.
But, where is the imposition of a duty upon somebody to enforce this Act?
The Railway Commission will enforce it.

If the Railway
Commission see fit to enforce it.

That is what we have
them for.

But, is there a
direct clause in this Act for its enforcement? We will shortly be dealing with clause 42, which refers to the employment of counsel in the public interests. According to this clause the board may apply to the Minister of Justice to instruct counsel.

That is not at all for
the enforcement of the Act.

Of course, there
may be provisions later for enforcing the . Act, but so far its enforcement is all done incidentally. It would be well for us to know the manner in which the board is to enforce this Act, and who should be held responsible for its enforcement. I dealt with the question in the House the other day, in connection with another Act. I also attended some of the meetings of the special
committee which had this matter under consideration, andrnet some of the men representing the brotherhoods. They said the great question with them was the enforcement of the Railway Act.
Why did they notmention that to the committee?

They did mention it, and I mentioned it also. I mention it now, and I hope the minister will consider it, so that we may have a direct and specific clause in the Act indicating that it is the dtity of the Railway Commission, or the Attorney General of Canada, or somebody else, to enforce the Act. It should not be left to any one to go before the board and make an application that the Minister of Justice appoint counsel to conduct an investigation in .order to bring out the facts in the public interest. This should be done by the Railway Commission of its own motion, and it should have power to employ special counsel at any time, and the duty should be imposed upon it to enforce and administer this law.

I understand that the
hon. gentleman wants to have a public officer appointed whose duty it is to enforce the railway law of Canada. I am afraid he would have to have a whole army of public officers, as these matters come up in every portion of Canada. There are plenty of powers given to somebody. If the hon. gentleman will look at sections 43 and 44 he will find that 43 provides for a stated case to go to the Supreme Court and 44 gives effect to the 'judgment of other courts. Then section 49 provides that any court in Canada having the proper jurisdiction can make a decision of the board a rule of court, and then it can be worked -out the same as any Tule of codrt would be in any province in Canada. You go on to sections 51 and 52 and these provide for appeal and review. There is plenty of machinery, plenty of law. What my hon. friend wants is some officer whose duty ik>
is to see that the law is enforced and the machinery is put into motion. That is done *by the people in the different parts of Canada who are interested. I am a practising lawyer and a client comes to me and says: I feel that the railway company is not carrying out the law; I am damaged or I have a grievance against that railway company. On this I apply through the proper channel and call upon the company to remedy that grievance. If they fail to do so I take whatever action I may think necessary. If you appointed one officer to

carry out the law, you would never have it done, because you would have such a multiplicity of cases that it would he impossible to go on with them all. You might have an officer who would say to me:	I
do not think that your client's case has very much merit and I do not know why I should bother my head about pressing it. He might in that way take away from my* client the right which the law gives him.
We are getting along pretty well and I would be opposed to seeing an officer appointed who could take away 4 p.m. from the ordinary resident of Canada the rights which are guaranteed to him by the Railway Act. He has rights now which enable him to go to the courts and enforce those rights under the law and machinery of the Act if necessary.

My hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carviell) has stated my case in another way. He says that the enforcement of this Act rests mainly upon the private prosecutor or the person, who feels aggrieved; he must put the law in motion. It is all very well to allow that right to rest with the individual. His right is provided for and I have no objection to that. But I also want something else; I want to have the duty imposed upon the board to enforce the law or I want to do as they do in the	United
States-in legislation of this kind in the United States they insert a clause which says that it shall be the duty of the Attorney General of the United States to enforce this law, having in view the rights of the public. He is by the Act authorized to appoint special counsel, to engage experts and otAers who can supply him with information on the subject, and he is further voted a sum of money to be at his disposal at any time for the enforcement of the Act. We in Canada are passing Federal Acts year after year, some of them having very wide powers, but we make no provision for the enforcement of these Acts as they 'do in the United States. With regard to many of them, we are gradually finding a roundabout way of securing their enforcement. But I should like to see a provision inserted for the enforcement of this Act. There are many instances in which this Act ought to be enforced, but it is not enforced because there is no piovision for enforcing it. HVhen we are discussing these wide powers which are to be conferred-on the board we ought also to impose on the board the duty of enforcing 
the law. Representatives of the brotherhoods, as well as individuals all over the country, say that it has been hard to secure the enforcement of this law. That is the line of argument that we have heard, and I would ask the minister to tell us, either now or a little later on, how he proposes to strengthen the uses of this Railway Act to the puiblic by making provision for its adequate enforcement.

If this were an ordinary Act that was only enforced through court proceedings there would be a good deal to be said in favour of my hon. friend's contention. But the object in establishing the Board of Railway Commissioners was not to make it a court, but to keep it as far away from being a court as we possibly could. . It was to be a quick and ready tribunal before which anybody could state his case. When I was Minister of Railways the question of the appointment of a public prosecutor was urged many times, but in discussing it with the then Chairman and with a great many public men, who have large business interests in shipping, etc., I found that none of them wanted to have a public prosecutor appointed for this particular Act. Among the reasons for that opinion was the fear that it would be surrounded by all the formalities and red tape of a court, and that the ordinary individual would of necessity be compelled eventually to approach that court through the public prosecutor. The object of establishing this Commission was that any person, even a widow with a grievance about a crossing on her farm, could appeal, by letter, perhaps, without gqing before the tribunal at all, and get substantial justice. Hundreds and hundreds of cases have been disposed of merely by a letter from the secretary to the railway company. The difficulty about appointing a public prosecutor would be that we would possibly get into a condition in which we might as well not have a railway commission at all, but a regular court, to try these cases. This Board hears counsel in any case that is brought before it if the applicant desires to be represented by counsel, but at the same time the humblest individual in Canada can go before the Board, state his or her case, and have it decided. '

I agree with what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Graham) says, but he does not meet my case. I do not ask for a public prosecutor. I ask that the duty be imposed on somebody to enforce this Act. I propose to make it the duty of this expensive organization, the

Board of Railway Commissioners, .to enforce it and to see that justice is done in any case where an individual brings before it a case of injustice. The enforcement of federal laws should not be left to the individual who feels aggrieved. We trust to the Minister of Customs to see that the customs law is obeyed and that the revenue is not defrauded. That minister makes prosecutions, and sometimes calls in, as he has a right to call in, the Minister of Justice to assist him. Under this Act the duty is not laid upon the Board of Railway Commissioners to enforce this Act. I ask that the Act shall say who is responsible for its enforcement. I am anxious to avoid, so far as possible, all red tape.

Has my hon. friend
heard of a case in Canada since the Commission was created in which it has not enforced any order that was made?
My hon. friend is talking about orders. I want enforcement of the law, not of orders.
Do you want it enforced without being heard?
No, it will be heard.
Then they will enforce it.
Who will enforce it?
The Railway Commission.

It is one of the representations of the brotherhoods that there is lots of power but none of that direct enforcement which the people of the United States are finding necessary in connection with their federal legislation. I want some provision for the enforcement of the Act. If I cannot do any better, I shall submit the clause in the transportation law of the United States which places responsibility for the enforcement of the Act.
If the hon. member will draft a clause he will consider 'it when we have gone through the Bill. It will have to come at the end anyway.

I know that in the
United States many Acts passed by Congress Wave such a clause as the hon. member has mentioned, but it would-be impossible to apply such a clause to this Bill. However, we will be glad to consider any clause he may draft.
The hon. member has not mentioned one case where the railway commission have not enforced the law.

I will give you
cases, and they have been mentioned before the -special committee.
Where the board was asked to act and did not?

No, but cases
where there was difficulty in getting any enforcement of the Act.
If the hon. member will put his suggestion in concrete form we can consider it.

I will put it in concrete form, and it will be the first time in our fifty years of history that we have put direct responsibility on somebody for the enforcement of the laws of this country.
I spoke the other day about the attainment of national unity. They -are attaining national unity in the United States by federal enforcement of federal law. One great thing about their constitution ias compared with ours-and I am not -saying which is better- is that the President o-f the United- States has very large powers, and so has the Atr tomey General of the United States, for the enforcement of federal laws. I will -submit later on a specific proposal in thi-s direction.

The municipality has power, under -provincial- legislation, to -pass laws with relation to the cutting and destruction of weeds. Take that as a concrete case. A serious growth of weeds on a railway right of w-ay running through a municipality is

a serious menace to the surrounding farms. Every company shall cause thistles and all noxious woods growing on the right of way, and upon land of the company adjoining the railway, to be cut down or to he rooted out and destroyed each year, before such thistles or weeds have sufficiently matured to seed.
If a railway company failed to carry out the provisions of this section, application could be made to the Board of Railway Commissioners for action in the matter. On section 49-rule of court:

I have strong doubt whether this Parliament -has power to say that the Supreme Court of a province shall or shall not do a certain thing, or that the registrar of a province, who is purely a provincial officer, shall or shall not do a certain thing. That was the answer I received.

I agree with the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell). The fact that such orders have been made and put through in the past is no indication of the legal right to make such provisions in this Bill. At some time, in a very important case, the question will be raised as to the right of making the decisions of the Board of Railway Commissioners a rule of our provincial courts. The matter will form a subject of consideration, and possibly there will be a decision against , the right of those courts to accept such rulings. It is the duty of the Minister of Justice to communicate with the attorney generals of the different provinces and ask them to pass ancillary legislation to make this effective. While the Minister of Justice reviews legislation passed by the different provinces, and, if necessary, calls the attention of the Provincial Attorney General to the

validity of any measure, and also informs him whether the legislature have attempted to exceed their jurisdiction, there is no such revising authority over Dominion legislation.

We have reached one stage further so far as the public interest is concerned. The jurisdiction of the provinces over certain matters has been called into question by two able lawyers, one from the New Brunswick courts and one from Nova Scotia. We may have to make provision in connection with federal legislation for the establishment of federal courts where these decrees will be recorded, and whereby they will be enforced. We are coming nearer to the issue that I have presented in this House. This shows how weak our system is after fifty years of experience. It has taken the people of the United States 150 years to find out that if they want to have effective legislation, and to protect the public interest, they must impose upon some federal officer or court the duty of enforcing that legislation, and they must constitute a federal court for registering their decrees and impose upon the officers of that federal court the duty of seeing that the decrees are carried out, not leaving their enforcement to the grace of some court or other organization in a province.
I shall be very glad to bring the matter to the attention of the Minister of Justice, and to inform him of the remarks made by the hon. members for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) and Pictou (Mr. Macdonald).

That the Commission hereby created shail have authority to inquire into the management of the business of all common carriers subject to the provision of this Act, and shall keep itself informed as to the manner and method in which the same is conducted-

That is the Interstate
Commerce Commission.

-and shall have the right to obtain from such common carriers full and complete information necessary to enable the Commission to perform the duties and carry out the objects for which it was created, and the Commission is hereby authorized and required to execute and enforce the provisions of this Act;-
That is what I want in this country. I desire a provision inserted that the Railway Commission shall be required to enforce the provisions of this Bill, and I have not got it yet. -and upon request of the Commission it shall he the duty of any district attorney of the United States to whom the Commission may apply to institute in the proper court and to prosecute under the direction of the Attorney General of the United States all necessary proceedings for the enforcement of the provisions of this Act, and for the punishment of all violations thereof, and the costs and expenses of such prosecution shall be paid out of the appropriation for the expenses of the courts of the United States; and for the purposes of this Act the company shall have power to require, by subpoena, the attendance and testimony of witnesses and the production of all books, papers, tariffs, contracts, agreements and 'documents relating to any matter under investigation.



We have no such provision, in our Act, and I again direct the attention of the Minister of Railways to it and ask him, in all fairness, to consider this question; and I ask him to ask the Minister of Justice and the Prime Minister whether it is not time that he should enact for Canada a similar provision for the enforcement of our laws. We have spent a lot of time on this measure and I compliment the minister on the excellent Act which has been framed. I say that it is deficient in the essential that no provision is made for its enforcement.

I must confess that I
[DOT]have never read the United States Intercommerce law ais carefully as my hon. friend, and I do not profess to know what the provisions are, and I have been wondering if that Act goes as far as our does.

In many ways it does
not.
There is no power that our railway commission does not possess in regard ito requiring the railway companies to do anything that can be conceived.

But where is
the provision compelling them to do it?

They have the power
to make rules and regulations. If a railway company is not observing the law and is granting exceptional 'advantages to one company over another-discrimination in traffic or in rates, or anything of that kind -the Board of Railway Commissioners has absolute power to take action. This Aot was in force before I came to Parliament, and I have been before this board a great many times, and I 'have never heard a suggestion that it does not enforce its decree and orders, and I cannot understand why there should be any necessity for a provision of this kind.
The commission would be useless if it did not enforce its orders.
The hon. gentleman from Oarleton (Mr. Carvell) is talking about decrees. They enforce the decrees, but supposing they do not make the decrees?

I will give an illustration. I got a letter within the last three weeks from a gentleman in New Brunswick, not .in my own constituency, pointing out the fact that a certain railway crossing was not protected and that something should be provided in the way of gates or guards. I at onee sent the letter on to the railway company, and asked them to give it their

consideration. I received a courteous letter from them, stating that they would hand it over to their traffic department .and would give me an answer. I have not received their decision yet, but if they fail to do what the people think they should do, all I have to do is to go to the Board of Railway Commissioners and if they order the company to put on guards or gates or watchmen, the commission will enforce such an order. It seems to me there is nothing to argue about.
We have given them absolute power to do every conceivable thing in regard to the railways.
I have never heard of a case where the board has not adjudicated on any matter submitted to them, and if they decide that a person is entitled to relief that relief is granted.

This is an attempt to draw a red herring across the trail.
I am not suggesting that the board has not the power, but in many cases they do not take action.
The hon. gentleman admits they have the power.

Yes, but there
is no provision that they must- exercise this power. If somebody calls their attention to it they may do it. The United States Act provides that the commission shall keep themselves posted in regard to the requirements of that Act.

The hon. gentleman
has not given us a case where they have not enforced it.

I will give cases [DOT] later on, but I want to deal with general principles to begin with. I say that the Railway 'Commission should be empowered and ordered to enforce this Act, and that they should have the means placed at their disposal to carry out the orders. We could have the Act enforced if the Minister of Justice would appoint an attorney to look after its enforcement. I place this point before the people of the country as the difference 'between our Railway Act and the Railway Act of the United States.
I would like to address a meeting of the farmers of this country, who are studying this question of transportation very closely, and point out to them the difference between the two Acts in the power of enforcement and the protection of the public rights. It should not he left to somebody, or to the Board itself, to ask for the ap-

pointment of counsel to assist in enforcing the law. It should he the duty of the Board to enforce the law. If permanent counsel are required I would not have any objection to their appointment, but I do say the responsibility should be with the Board. Apparently it is a hard thing to persuade this committee to see the question in that light, but that was the experience of the United States.
Will my hon. friend tell us when the Interstate Commerce Commission was appointed?
Many years before ours.
My impression was that ours was first.

I am quite sure the United States Commission was first. In any event, they have had a wider experience than ours. I would ask hon. gentlemen to secure a copy of the United States Act, and study it. Clause after clause of our Act has been taken bodily from it.

As I understand the point made by the hon. member, he thinks this Commission, or court, should institute proceedings before itself. To my mind, that is not practicable in Canada. If it were done I fear the court would very soon lose its weight, influence and respect. I think it is as well ito leave the matter as it is, and when any one has a grievance let the question be taken up in the proper manner before the Board. Perhaps I would go to the extent of agreeing with the hon. gentleman that there might be a public officer appointed whose duty it would be to institute proceedings before the Board.

It is very hard to convince those able lawyers in regard to the jurisdiction of courts. I am only an ordinary layman-

For the instruction of the distinguished legal light from Nova Scotia (Mr. McKenzie), who was a judge and who knows a good deal about courts, let me direct his attention to the following:
And the Commission is hereby authorized and required to execute and enforce the provisions of this Act; and upon the request of the Commission, it shall he the duty of any district attorney of the United States to whom the Commission may apply to institute in the proper court, and to prosecute under the

direction of the Attorney General of the United States all necessary proceedings for the enforcement of the provisions of this Act and for the punishment of all violations thereof, and the costs and expenses of such prosecution shall be paid out of the appropriation for the expenses of the courts of the United States.

But there is nothing to show whose duty it is to enforce the law. My hon. friend from North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) says we do not need any court, or we are imposing an unnecessary duty on the commission. In the United States they impose certain duties on the commission in connection with the enforcement of the law. They go further -and say:

And penalties are imposed and fines collected. We have not that clear-cut direction for the enforcement of our Act. It has taken me twenty-five years to get a hearing in this House in connection with the enforcement of the federal law. I have been side-tracked twenty times by men who were Ministers of Justice, trying- to evade this point. However, this condition of affairs will not continue much longer. After fifty years' experience, I think we ought to change the law in this direction, and I again draw the attention of the Minister of Railways to the fact that he may make this excellent Act of his still more effective by including in it a provision for its enforcement similar to the provision in the United States Act.

The hon. gentleman raises a tu'penny-ha'penny case.

I admit the board may make an order, and when they order that so-and-so shall happen the public will be protected; or, when the Attorney General of Canada sees fit to engage counsel to prosecute the case the public will be projected. But again, if that does not happen, who is to protect the public? I appeal to my hon. friend (Mr. Wright) who is a .common, ordinary farmer-

A real farmer.

Well we will say an ordinary farmer. I am a very poor farmer myself; I have not got to the high exaltation of being a farmer yet, but a farmer can see that it is one thing to make a law and quite another to enforce it. This is a good law and the farmers of the West

as well as the farmers of Ontario are reading up these laws. We see the necessity of improving this law, and this is a vastly improved law, but' it must be enforced. They have passed a law in the United States for the enforcement of railway legislation. They not only make, provision in that law for its enforcement but they provide the money and they put the duty on the railway commission to keep themselves posted as to the objects of the law. Tt is their duty to enforce it and to go to the district attorneys throughout the United States and through them to lay information before the court. Why should there not be provision for the enforcement of this law which is based on the Inter-state Commerce Act?

I want to go back to my little case of a railway company that fails to keep proper guards in place at the highway crossing and I want to ask my hon. friend a question. Would he want a provision in the law that a farmer, or a man travelling along the road, could write to this officer representing the Attorney General and have him take charge of the case and present it to the board and then have the board issue an order. Does he want to have some official to see that the
5 p.m. order is enforced, or does he only want to see that the order of the board is enforced?

I only want to see that the law is enforced and I want to see that when the order is made it is carried out. I want the duty put upon somebody to carry out the law whether it is done by a clause similar to this clause in the Interstate Commerce Act or otherwise. It is very clear what I want.

I am going to get it ready but it takes a great deal of time to get an argument before this committee.
You have to prepare the ground first?

You sure have.

I want the board to protect the public rights. The Hon. gentleman (Mr. McKenzie) says that we are satisfied with the way the Criminal Code is being enforced. Are we? I am not satisfied with the way that federal law is being enforced by local attorneys in various parts of the country. When I had this question up in another case the leader of the Opposition asked me why I did not go to Mr. Foy for the enforcement of a certain Act in Ontario. I said in reply:	You cannot
always get enforcement of the Criminal Code by provincial authorities. I want to give another specific instance of that. We have a law against combinations in restraint of trade. The whole prosecution devolves upon the private pro-secutor. It is the old story; unload it on the private individual. Of course this federal Act declares that combines a-re illegal, but it does not say that it shall be the duty of the Attorney General of Canada to enforce this law against combines, nor is there a sum of money set apart for the enforcement of the law or the prosecution of combines against the public interest. Day after day we are passing Acts in this Parliament and making no provision for their enforcement. Of all the humbug Acts that were ever passed by this Parliament, the Acts in connection with federal elections are the most notable. Has there ever been- any prosecution of any kind under those Acts? There have been lots of saw-offs and the people know all about that, but there has never been any enforcement of the election law of this country. That we leave to somebody else. I am talking right outside of this House now and to the people of Canada, and I say that when you are making laws in the public interest you must also make provision for their enforcement. I will give another instance where the United States has had to resort to a special federal law. They never could secure the enforcement of the law against some of the worst crimes that were ever committed in the United States in connection with labour troubles. There were lots of statutes in the various states against the perpetration of such crimes but no enforcement of those statutes. The danger to the public from the perpetration of those crimes was so great and the in-

ability to get any of these laws enforced so evident that the Congress and Government of the United States were driven to the adoption of a subterfuge. They passed an Act providing that whoever employed a railway train for the conveyance of dynamite, or travelled on a railway train for the purpose of committing a crime of this kind, would be liable to be indicted in a court and tried for the crime which he committed. These crimes were put down in the United States by the enforcement of a federal law by the Attorney General of the United States, who had all the resources of the country at his back. They got prosecutions and convictions, and they put an end to these crimes. You ask: Why do you not get your criminal law enforced by means of provincial officials and courts? At times you get it and get substantial justice, but there are many cases where you cannot get that substantial justice because you cannot bring about the enforcement of the law. Again I come -back to my argument that if this law is to be effective you must make provision for its enforcement and impose the duty primarily on the commission itself and also on the Attorney General of th* country, because, perhaps, proceedings in a federal court may yet have to come. That is the question and it must be specifically dealt with in this Act.

Do I understand the hon. member to advocate the establishment of two complete sets of legal machinery in the country, from constables up to Supreme Court, one for the Dominion and one for the various provinces?

Effective means of enforcing the law.
