Secondly, the old law provided that there should not be a deviation of more than so much a milo "from the plan as filed." That, I think, means filed at the office of the registrars of deeds at different places. The new section provides that that plan shall .also he filed with the Board. It means the filing of two plans instead of one, and cuts down the deviation from a mile to half a mile.
On section 186-Use of spur for another industry.

At the beginning of this section, after the word " notwithstanding," the following words were struck out: " any agreement or arrangement made."
TMr. Carvell.]

This is a new clause, which is not found in the Railway Act. In general terms, it provides that the Board shall have the power to allow a person or company to use a spur line that has been constructed in connection with the business of another person or company.

Section agreed to.
On section 193-lands of other companies:

The last two subsections of this section have been reconstructed. The object is to prevent unnecessary cuttings into cities and towns and the multiplication of highway crossings. Subsection 4 gives the board power to order the company to take the proceedings provided for under the old section, and subsection 5 gives the board still further power as to ordering the joint use of rights of way.

Section agreed to.
On section 197-board may order compensation in certain cases:
This is a new provision; it seems to he a reasonable one. It is in conformity with the law that has existed in Ontario for some time.

The Board has the right to give the railway company occupation of whatever land may be necessary, but if there be valuable minerals under the railway line that cannot be mined because of the construction of the railroad, the company must pay compensation to the owners. I believe that the board have the right to assess damages.

Section agreed to.
On section 198-examination of mine workings:
I see that the railway company is supposed to give the owner of the mine twenty-four hours' notice before, entering upon his lands.
That is enough.

Having obtained permission of the Board, the company has the right to enter upon the lands and see whether any condition exists which would be detrimental to the safety of the railway. They have the right, not to remove or change anything, hut simply to investigate.

Section agreed to.
On section 200-where more ample space required:

In the thirty-fifth line, after the word "may," the words

"whether before or after the railway has been opened for the carriage of traffic" have been added. In subsection 7, line 6, after the word "railway," the words "but the deposit with the board and with the registrar of deeds shall be made as in this section provided" have been added. These are the only changes.

Under the existing law, the railway company has to file a plan and book of reference, having the right to take whatever land may be therein included. This provision in the present Bill leaves it open to the railway company, even after the railway has commenced to operate, to file a new plan and book of reference and take more land. Such a provision may be necessary, and I do not know that I specifically object to it; but it is a rather drastic provision.

It is often very necessary for them to take more land. They would have to pay for it.
Mr. CARVEI.L:	Subsection 7 provides
that:
The deposit with the hoard and with the registrar of deeds shall he made as in this section provided.
That is, the company have to make a new deposit, new plans, new book of reference, and have a new arbitration if they cannot come to an agreement with the owner of the land. This gives the railway companies very large powers.
The meaning is made more clear. .

Section agreed to.	,
On section 202-Obtaining materials for construction or operation:
Subsection 6 is new. It gives the powers of the board.

This section means that a railway company will have the right to lay a temporary track for the purpose of bringing material for the use of the railway. They lay that track practically under such directions as the board may issue. After the track has been used and the material provided, then it can bfi taken up and the company would have to pay as compensation whatever damages the owner of the land had suffered, but they do not have to expropriate. They are given the right to go on the land temporarily.

Section agreed to.
On section 206-Order of judge may be had:

This section has practically been reconstructed. The following proviso has been added:
Provided that where any person interested is absent from the district or county in which the lands lie, or is unknown, the judge may order such substitutional service of notice as he deems proper or may dispense with notice.

Suppose a man died and left a will and all' the terms of the will had not been carried out, and on account of minors or something of that sort, there was no person in a position to give a deed; tnis section provides that the trustee, or the executor under the will, or some person who occupies a fiduciary position is, in this case, authorized to give a deed, but the change is made that this can be done only by an order of the court. It also provides what notice must be given before the court can exercise the rights conferred upon it.

Section agreed to.
On section 214-disagreement.

Mr. Chairman, I think
the sections are being run through too fast. I would like them to be read in French. As we are endeavouring to improve the law, I would like to have time to read over the sections in order to see what they are.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
If the hon. member
wishes a special section to be read, I shall be glad to read it.

If there is -any special section (that the hon,. member would like to have read, I am sure we shall be very glad to listen to it and have him make whatever remarks he pleases in regard to it; butt might I respectfully ask him to consider the fact that this Bill was before a special committee of this House for seven or eight weeks? During that time people from all parts of (the co,untry representing different organizations and institutions, were invited to come, and did come, before the committee. They were given every opportunity of placing their views before the committee. As chairman of that committee, I want to take this opportunity of thanking the members on both sides of the House for the splendid work they did in ,assisting in every way possible to bring about suitable legislation; I hope the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Boulay) will not press his request.

Not only do I press my
request, but I insist upon its being granted, because, not belonging to the Railway Committee I have until now had no opportunity

of studying the Bill. There were several amendments that I was going to suggest when this Bill came into Committee of the Whole. I find now that the Bill is being put through in a very hurried manner, and I have no opportunity of suggesting amendments or even of knowing what the sections are. If the committee is willing to set some of the sections aside for discussion later on, I am willing to agree to that. There are quite a number of sections that have not been amended and that surely should be amended.
I am sure the committee will be very glad to hear later on all the amendments that the hon. member for Rimouski cares to lay before it.

If the hon. gentleman
will pick out the clauses, we can take them up.
If the hon. gentleman will mention the clauses, we will reconsider them.
But all the other clauses were adopted. Important objections might have been miade to clauses 9 and 10, but they have been adopted.

Even though, they were
passed by the committee, if the hon. gentleman desires to discuss them, he should have an opportunity.
There would be no objection to that.

Section agreed to.
Section 215-Notice of expropriation to be served:

The words
"preliminary to proceeding to arbitration to fix compensation or damages'* have been added in this section, and paragraph (e) is added so that the owner may have explicit notice of the rights of the company, and as to what he must do, so that he will not be prejudiced by letting the time go by in which he must act.

I think there has been a material change in that section. Any solicitor who has had much experience in expropriation proceedings must have found a great injustice in the present law in this regard. The present law provides that the railway company shall do certain things- they must serve notice upon the owner, giving a description of the lands to be taken, or the powers intended to be exercised with regard to any land therein described, fMr. Boulay.]
and the notice must contain a declaration of readiness to pay a certain sum or rent as the case may be, as compensation for such lands or for such damages. But there is no provision to force the company to carry on the proceedings to a finality, and many a man has been held up for months -the railway companies have obtained an order from the judge and got possession through the sljpriff, and allowed the mat^r to drift. Very few are able to realize what their real damages are by simply being told that the railway company is going to build a railway across the land. The railway must be constructed before the owners can ascertain their damages. This section provides that either the railway company or the owner shall have the right to have the compensation fixed by arbitration. It is one of the greatest boons that has been granted to the landowners in the whole Act, because it puts them in a position, immediately after the notice has been given, or within ten days, if the railway company do not proceed to have damages ascertained by arbitration, to compel them to move.

Section agreed to.
On section 216-Certificate of surveyor or engineer:

The only change is adding, after the word "w1m>
" in the third line, the words " is not interested in the land, or in the amount of compensation or damages." The hon. member for North Oxford will remember that, in the reprint, they appeared to have marked the . clauses one number ahead of the numbers appearing on the old Bill. One clause was dropped and that disarranged all the others. In paragraph (c), in the first line, the words " what sum is " have been added.

Section agreed to.
On section 217-service by publication:

There is an important amendment to this section. At the end of subsection 3 the following words are added:
And in such other newspapers, if any, as the judge may direct.
Does that provide that the publication shall be made in both languages in Quebec, or only in English? Nothing is said about it in the Bill.

The hon. gentleman will notice that subsection 3 says:
The judge shall order a notice as aforesaid, hut without such certificate, to be inserted three times in the course of one month in a newspaper published in the district.
If it is in the French district, it would naturally be published in the French paper, or if there is no French newspaper published in the district, then it would be published in a French newspaper in the adjoining district or county, and in such other newspaper, if any, as the judge may direct.
Mr. BOULAY": That is not sufficient to insure that it would be published in French. There might be a French and an English paper, and if the company chose to publish only in English, that would be their own business.
The judge has the decision as to the paper in which it shall be published.

But supposing the judge does not say anything about it, or suppose he decides it shall only be published in English, where will be the fair play for the other section of the population in the province of Quebec?
Do you think the judge would show any partiality in that regard?
Not in Quebec.
I think it better that it should be published in both languages in the province of Quebec, instead of leaving it to the decision of the judge.
It might well be left to the judge.

The law provides for the manner of publication of such matter in the province of Quebec, and there is no reason why a Bill of this kind should not also provide for it. If there were a general proviso to1 the effect that it should be published in both languages in the province of Quebec, it would be different. Perhaps we might go back and insert some such clause in one of the first sections of the Bill.

There is some reason
for what the hon. gentleman says, but I would not restrict it to the province of Quebec, because there are parts of Ontario where at least half the population is French. I would support an amendment providing that where two papers are published, one in French and one in English, the advertisement should appear in both.
What I have said about the province of Quebec might also apply to the province of New Brunswick.

There is a great deal, of course in what the hon.. member for Rimouski (Mr. Boulay) says. In case the owner of the land is absent, or cannot be reached, the notice should be published in such a way that it would cover him. If there were a French paper in the district it would be only fair that the notice should be published in. French also. It would not involve any great expense or difficulty. I think it would be better to provide for this specially, rather than include it in the section regarding definitions, because there you might have to apply it to all notices, and there may be many cases in which it is not necessary to publish or serve a notice in both languages. I had a somewhat similar case a few years ago. Under the law of New Brunswick which has not been changed for a great many years and which was practically the law of Canada prior to about 1890, there was no provision for service upon a man by publication. In the case I refer to, it looked

at one time as if a very great injustice was going to be done, because the railway company made an application without any notice at all, and the parties interested had no knowledge of the matter until after it was settled.

In the province of Quebec all legal notices in addition to being published in the local papers are published in the Quebec Official Gazette, which is printed in French and in English. I would suggest that these notices be published in the Quebec Official Gazette.

I think it would be as well to let the clause stand, so that the minister may give it further consideration.
Section stands.
On section 218-Notice may be abandoned :

There are several important changes in this section. In the sixth line the words " suffered and costs " have been added. In the seventh line, the words " and such damages shall be fixed and such costs taxed by the judge, or as he directs," are added. Subsection 3, paragraphs (a) and (b) and subsection 4 have been added.

The material change is this: The original Act provided that in case of abandonment the company shall be liable to the person notified for all damages and' costs incurred by him in consequence of such notice .and abandonment. You will see that in the new Act it is changed to make it explicit that he shall be indemnified for all damages and costs incurred by him. The reason is that there has been a good deal of litigation in various parts of Canada, both under the Dominion and local Railway Acts over the question as to whether the landowner was entitled to his costs or to his costs and damages. There have been decisions both ways. The object of the section is to make it clear that the landowner should get both damages and costs. Subsection 2 provides that in case they want further land, they can abandon the former notice and issue a new notice, but if an arbitration had taken place as to the value of the first land taken, that may be used as evidence in the second arbitration in so far as it is applicable.
It is to the advantage of the individual?	*

Yes, all these changes are intended to inure to the benefit of the landowner.
On section 219-Arbitrator; if sum offered not accepted; appointment of arbitrator; notice; service by publication:

In the second line after the word "or" the words "where service is made by advertisement" have been added. After the word "it" in the fifth line, the following words have been added:
Either party may apply to the judge of the county court of the county in which the lands lie, or, in the province Of Quebec or in any other part of Canada where there is no county court, to a judge of the Superior Court for the district or place in which the lands lie, to determine the compensation to be paid as aforesaid.
Does the question of language come in there in connection with these advertisements?
The advertisements were mentioned in connection with the clause that has been left over.
Will that apply to 219 as well?
I do not know that it would, because the added words have to do with the application and not with the question of language.
At the beginning of the clause it says "where service is made by advertisement." Will that 'advertisement be in an English paper or in a French paper? How would that affect a French district?

That was, discussed on section 217, and the clause was allowed to stand for the purpose of providing that if there be both an English and a French paper it should be published in both. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Descarries) suggested that it also might be published in the official Gazette in Quebec which is published both in English and French.
Will that apply to section 219?
Yes, because 219 is a necessary corollary of 217.
Then 219 had better stand?
No, put in a clause to cover the whole.

The committee will appreciate the convenience of publishing a notice

that the people will understand. There are some districts where there are no English papers at all.
In that case you will have to publish it in French.

There is only one suggestion that I would likb to make if section 219 is to stand, and it is that in the case of an absentee landowner, six days' notice in a newspaper is absolutely useless. I would suggest that the minister consider the possibility of giving the judge power to extend the time of notice, as well as to shorten it. You will see that subsection 3 of section 219 says:-
Provided that the judge may dispense with, or shorten the time or times for, the publication of the notice in any such case in which he deems it proper.
The judge should have the power to dispense with, shorten or lengthen the time.
It says that six days' notice shall be given by the company to the opposite party.

And vice versa. The law has been changed. Either party may move for an arbitration. The notice does not make much difference to the railway companies, (because the railway companies are vitally interested; they have their solicitors and engineers; they are always ready and six days' notice to them is just as good as a month. But that will not suit the landowner.
9 p.m. Mr. COCHRANE: How many days would you extend it?
I should say ten days' notice.
Change it from six to ten.

A farmer out in the country gets notice from a railway company that they are going in a short time to expropriate his land, and it takes him three or four days to wake up and realize what is going to happen. Then he goes to town and looks up his lawyer and it takes his lawyer some time to wake up. A notice of ten days is short enough.
Make it ten.
Will you move that amendment?

Yes, I will move:
That the word "six" be changed to "ten" in subsections 2. and 3 wherever it occurs.

If there is to be an amendment made to the subsection I would like to suggest that provision be made by which a judge could direct that notice should be given to some relative, or to some other party, who would be in a position to know something about the absent proprietor. In the ordinary legal process, where you have to deal with absentees and you apply for substitute service of the documents or notice, the judge, in providing as to the publication in a newspaper of the advertisement calling attention to the matter that is to be served or that is under adjudication, usually provides that in the event of any relative or representative of the absentee being present he shall be notified
Supposing there is not one there?

Then you leave it to the discretion of the judge. You go to the judge and he gives an order allowing you to serve the absentee by giving notice in a newspaper for ten days. That may, or may not, be effectual at all. It is usually a fictitious thing any way. I think that my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell) would agree that there is no reason why a judge should not exercise that same discretion which he exercises in an ordinary case in which he is dealing with substitute service of notice on some other person who is connected, or has some relation, with the absent owner of the land. This would be a real notice; in the other case it would not.

I would agree with that. I am speaking with a considerable personal knowledge of these things because I had a case within the last two years where the landowner was an absentee. Our statute in New Brunswick did not require notice at all when he was an absentee. The arbitration was practically over before we knew anything about it. Fortunately, we were able to get wise in time to get in there and we pretty nearly got our rights.
Would the absentee not have an agent in the district?

No, lots of men who own land are away; men are in the West, they are at the front or they are anywhere in the world. In a great many cases western lands are owned by people in the East. The railway company can honestly say: we have made diligent inquiry and have been unable to locate the real owner. It is only right that the landowner whose land is being

taken should have notice, or that every reasonable attempt should he made to give him notice.
Would you suggest some amendment to cover it?

I can show one case
where the -addition of two words would materially affect it. We might say "-the judge may dispense with or shorten or lengthen the time."

Why not change
" shorten " to " lengthen?"

There should be
some further words there providing for personal service upon the agent of the owner or something of that kind. I should -like the clause to be allowed to -stand.
Will you prepare an amendment?

I will.
Section stands.
On section 220-Judge the sole arbitrator.
This is quite a change. It provides that the judge alone becomes the arbitrator, unless in a case where he is personally interested, when he can appoint another judge. That is -a complete change.

The change is not
objectionable i-s it?	.

I am not so sure about that. I think the landowners in the vicinity are -perhaps better judges of the value of land, or the damages that would be sustained by a farmer through, having -a railway cro-ss his -property, than a judge would be. This is taking away altogether the principle of arbitration.	.
The judge would have to hear the case.

Under the old law he
did not.
He would under this.

He would under this.
I should rather leave the law as it stands, and let this matter remain in the hands of the arbitrators. A lot of horse sense is required in settling the amount of damage in such a case, and I would prefer to leave it to the arbitrators. I doubt very much if the ordinary judge would toe able to appreciate the probable- damage as well as would men living in the neighbourhood. I have had some experience with judges in

these things, and I must say that, from the standpoint of the owner, I would prefer the man who I know knows all about it. It is a very serious thing.

Would not a judge in a ease of that kind call in witnesses to prove the value of the land? I cannot agree that the judge would not toe a pretty good arbitrator. ,The ordinary county court judge with us is a very ordinary chap before he -becomes a county court judge. He is generally a practising barrister, and has to do with these things.
Sometimes he does and sometimes he does not.

He knows a good deal
about every de-al from a horse trade up.
Many of these men come from town-s and know nothing about damage to land.

There are many eases where the county court judge would not be a suitable man. I do not think it would be advisable to make this change; it would -be much better to leave it to so-me arbitrator who, by reason of his particular knowledge, would be suitable. Some old county court judges would make very gotfd men, but remember that they are all new men at some time, and many of the new men coming in as county court judges are about the worst men you could get for that sort of work. The present law is better.
I do not know; I feel like trusting the judge.
The judge has power to appoint arbitrators.
Under what section?
Only in case he is interested, and that is the time when he should not appoint another man.

Under the old law the
judge appoints one man and each side has a right to appoint one, and so you get a pretty fair tribunal.
The judge has the same power under this clause, has he not?

No. The judge is the
arbitrator under this law; if he is interested in the case, he appoints another judge.
I w-as not present at the meeting of the committee when these sections went through. I did not think for a moment

that you would take from the farmer the right to be represented by another farmer on that arbitration. I object very strongly to that course. The average judge has n,o conception of the amount of damage done to a farm by its 'being traversed by a railway.
I would not for $1,000 haye a railway come across my farm-I suppose the judge would give me about $100, because he would not appreciate what the presence of that railway line on my farm meant. A farmer whose land is traversed by a railway line has to cross that line perhaps half a dozen times each day during the summer-and it is there, not for a year or two years, but for all time, for him and for his children, after him. By this provision we are taking away, without justification, one of the rights which, under the Railway Act, the citizen has had during the last forty years.
Under subsection 2, the judge has the power to call witnesses.
Certainly.

And make a
thorough investigation into the matter.

I realize that, but I do not think that a judge is in a position properly to appreciate the amount of damage that is occasioned to a farmer because of the presence of a railway line on his land. The farmer should have the right to be represented in that court by one of his own people-one of his own peers, I might say, who 'appreciate the real extent of the damage done.
They can give evidence to that effect.

In the case of land expropriated for Government purposes, the law formerly was that the value of the land and the damage sustained should be determined by a board of arbitrators, appointed permanently by the Dominion Government, who had long experience in dealing with cases of that kind. This method was abolished and a judge of the Exchequer Court was given jurisdiction in such matters. The judges of the Exchequer Court have become very competent in dealing with these cases, being familiar with the exceptional circumstances which, as the member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) points out, arise in a great many cases. But when County Court judges deal with these arbitrations, they are dealing with a class of cases entirely different from those that ordinarily come before them. They are not, therefore, the best authorities for determining such matters. The change proposed is,
I think, a very radical one, and my hon. friend is quite right in pointing out its importance and suggesting that the matter should be carefully considered.

Under this section a complete change is proposed in the method of arbitration in matters connected with the operation of railways. Formerly provision was made for three arbitrators; under this law provision is made for only one who, in the province of Quebec for instance, is to be a judge of the Superior Court. Under subsection 2, the decision of that judge is to be final; there is to be no appeal. Under section 224, the party whose property is expropriated has the right to present three experts or witnesses on his behalf, while in civil cases the party to a litigation has the right to produce five witnesses. The man whose property is taken from him by a railway company does not get the benefit of many of the advantages given to him by the ordinary courts. No doubt a judge is able to understand such matters better than the ordinary arbitrator; but valuation is a question not of law, but of experience. Many judges are not experienced in the valuation of land; they are not familiar with all the disadvantages which result to a farmer through his land being crossed by a railway. In view of the fact that only three witnesses are allowed to the person submitting a claim, I think that the provision is not fair; the section should not pass as it stands.

I wish to read to the committee the reasons given by Mr. Price, who prepared these clauses, for making the amendments proposed in the Bill. He says:	.
Arbitration proceedings generally. This part of the Act has been almost entirely remodelled and very materially altered. There [DOT] has been much complaint both from the companies and owners about the unsatisfactoriness and delays and excessive cost of arbitration proceedings, and the unsatisfactoriness of the appeal and proceedings allowed to impeach awards.
The County Court judge, and in the province of Quebec, a Superior Court judge, is now made arbitrator ex-officio. The costs' of the arbitration are left in his discretion.
The absurd provision that if the award was not made within a time fixed, the amount offered by the company should be taken to be the compensation, is abolished, but provision is made to prevent delay.
The number of expert witnesses is limited to three for any one party.
The unjust provision that the owner could not appeal unless the award was over $600, even though he might be entitled to many times as much, is amended so that he may appeal when he claims more than $600.

Wider powers are given the court in the appeal and except where more than 510,000 is involved only one appeal is allowed and no other proceedings can he taken to impeach the award.

It seems to be taking a very radical step to take away the right that the people have had in the past and to put this matter into the hands of a county court judge. While a county court judge may be a very creditable individual ;to try special cases, he may hold his court twenty-five or fifty miles away from where the railway crosses the land and where the damage accrues to the owner. All that he has before him is a plan or profile of the land; he does not understand the situation at all, and it would be very much better to have as arbitrator a person who knows the district and all the conditions. The Intercolonial railway goes through a man's farm close to where I live, and not a year passes but from three to five head of cattle aie killed. Last year this man had eight head of cattle killed on the railway crossing his farm.

Was he paid for the
damage?
No, the Intercolonial did not pay him a dollar.
Why?
Because they claimed they were not liable.
They do not pay for such damages.

I am positive that on that tarm alone during the past fifteen years twenty-five head of cattle have been killed. A judge living a distance away would not realize the great loss occasioned to a farmer residing in that particular locality. Where a railroad company wants to cross a farm with its railway it would be much better to have as arbitrator a man knowing the locality than any county court judge.
Does not the Intercolonial pay for animals killed?
They pay nothing.
That is not correct.

In ordinary cases of damage the facts are left to be decided by a jury composed of people selected from the locality in which the damage occurred, and that is generally conceded by all interested to be the better way of deciding the matter. It would be a mistake for this committee at this time to make this radical change in this section.

I do not care whether this section is changed back again or not. Although I am not a lawyer, I have had to make for other people a good many settlements for land damages, and I have never yet had occasion to go to arbitration. I have always foui^d the railway companies very reasonable, if they are approached properly. I am much surprised that the minister, if he does not keep up his fences, does not pay damages for cattle killed.
I think I can show by returns that the statement made was not correct.
That must be in other parts of Canada than in New Brunswick.
No, in New Brunswick too.
If a county court judge knows anything about his business, if he does not know the locality, he will visit it and make himself acquainted with it.

This question affects the owner of the land 'as well as the railway company. There are many things that affect the amount of damages, for instance, where the railway station might be located, where streams might have to be crossed, how the railway would run across a farm. While I have a good deal of confidence in our county court judges, many of them know very little about farm lands, and if a county court judge is to be the sole arbitrator, the whole matter is taken out of the hands of the owner of the land. The owner of the land should have some little say in the matter.
He has.

I quite agree with the
hon. member for South Ontario (Mr. William Smith), the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) and some others who have spoken on this matter. We ought to avoid putting into the Railway Act anything that will interfere with the rights of the owner of the land. I, perhaps, have as much experience as most men have with the disadvantages and inconveniences of getting into places across railway tracks, where the railway track crosses a farm between the home and the highway, and I would hesitate a long time before buying a farm with a track crossing between the farm buildings and the highway. Any railway company seeking a right of way should be compelled by arbitration to pay the owner of the land just and generous recompense for the privilege of crossing his farm, especially in that

way. A county court judge is not always to be relied upon to give a just judgment in matters of this character. Not intentionally would they be unfair, but such matters are out of their line of business, and in many cases they are quite unable to come to. a proper decision as to the value of the land which the railway company is asking for the privilege of crossing. The rights and interests of the farmer should be protected in a betteT way than, seems to be the case in this section.

We should be very careful before we make the change proposed in this section. The great complaint comes from the corporation, not from the individual farmer. The farmer asks what he thinks is- a reasonable damage on account of a railway going through his property, and if the corporation thinks his price is a little too high, it may take two or three years before the farmer can get a board of arbitration and have the question decided. There has been a good deal of trouble on this acount in some districts, and the delay has never been occasioned by the farmer. I have no complaint to make about county court judges, but I do not think they are the proper people to appoint as the sole arbitrators in cases of this kind. Any farmer who has a railway crossing his farm knows what the damage is. The railway companies sometimes seem to think that all lands, fruit and farm, are the same, and that they can run through every part of a province- paying the .same rate of damages. The old arbitration was better, where the individual farmer had an opportunity of having appointed on the board a man knowing something about the local conditions, the value of the land and so on.

Might I call
the committee's attention to the fact that changing this section will mean the changing of ten or twelve other sections of the Bill?

That is simple. There
is another -branch to this. In many cases railway companies go through timber lands in -the rear of a man's farm. I do not know that that would apply to Ontario as much as to some parts in the East, but you would never get -a county court judge to go out into the woods, .and travel through the right .of way, and examine the damage done. It would be impossible.

A Superior Court
judge in Montreal would not go there.

If you have an arbitration composed of farmers, they will take the trouble to go and look over the right of way. I had a case where the company offered $110 damages for going through timber land, and the arbitrators went out to the district, took a competent man with them, counted the stumps, figured the amount ,of lumber that had been taken, and that farmer got $1,200 .and costs. He would never have got that much from a county court judge in the world, because the judge would not go and look at it, and if you told him there was that much damage, he would not believe it.
But the farmer could take an expert out there, to value the damage.

But the judge would not believe it possible that the damage would amount to such a sum. ,In the case I referred to they brought in -a statement of the number of stumps, .and the diameter of them, and figured out the superficial feet, and there was a unanimous award of $1,200.

The same evidence
could have been produced before a county court judge.

But the judge would
not believe there was that much lumber growing on the right of way.
He could not help believing it.

I must protest. It
seems to me there is no -advantage in leaving it in the hands of the county court judge. Why should it be left to him?
To save expense.
Why take it out of the hands of the arbitration board, which we have had in the past, and put it in the hands of county court judges? Who asked for it?
The farmer.

I guess not. The companies have asked for it, and they put up the excuse. I remember of cases where there was delay after delay. The farmer was for months and months trying to hurry it up, and the company, with all their money behind them, tried to keep it back, because they thought they should only pay a certain amount.
That delay is fixed in a former section.

If it is fixed, why take it out of the hands of the arbitrator, and put it in the hands of the county court judge, who, perhaps, was never on a farm in his life? If a farmer in the country employed an expert who had an idea of the local value of land, and an idea as well of the damage caused by the railway running across his place, and placed the case before a county court judge who had no experience in such matters, I think it would be a great mistake.

I think the majority of cases of this kind are settled between the parties without going to arbitration. If the railway company and the owner of the land can agree, they do not require to go to arbitration, but, in the event of having to go to arbitration, surely it cannot be argued that a judge, who perhaps lives fifty or sixty miles from the seat .of trouble, could have as good a knowledge of it as men who go on the ground and examine it. It has been said that companies usually have to pay more when the cases are tried before arbitration. I do not think it will work that way always. I think you can get a just valuation of the damage actually caused. It may be as often in favour of the company as in favour of the individual, but where you have three men selected, one by the railway, one by the owner of the property, and the third appointed by the two as umpire, I think will work well.
That is the old law.

It should remain as it is. It seems to me a very much more just way of settling a matter of this kind, where the men who are going to appraise the damage go on the ground and examine it. A judge of the Superior Court is not going to run around examining lands here and there, and he would not know anything about their value if he did. He may know the law, but he would not know much about the value of timber or farm land, and it seems to me to be a mistake to change from the old system in this particular case.

I think it is always dangerous to make exceptions. There is always better safeguard and more protection for parties interested if they have their disputes disposed of by the old law. As far as arbitration is concerned, in the province of Quebec I do not see that there aTe any dangers. There may have been complaints. We have had many complaints in regard to judges; that is the reason we have so many jurisdictions. We start from the 
jurisdiction of the simple justice of the [DOT]peace np to the Supreme Court of Canada, and then we go to the foot of the Throne, to the Privy Council. I do not think human justice has been so perfect as to please all parties in this country, nor in any other country in the world. Something has been said in regard to the question of costs. If hon. members will look at the Quebec code of civil procedure they will find that every party is well protected, and even the railway companies, who are seeking to have this Bill passed, will be sorry for it after it becomes law, because judges may render decisions that .appear favourable to them, hut may he adverse to their interests, and they may be tied up. Section 411 of the Quebec .code reads as follows:
The court, of its own motion, or upon the application of either party, or the judge upon the application of either party may refer to the decision of the arbitrators, any case of dispute between relations, concerning partitions or other matters of fact, which is difficult for the court to appreciate, and also any other cases, if the parties consent to it.
I wil-l not read 'the next section, but it concludes in this way:
They may not award costs, unless the court has empowered them so to do.
. So that, if the court should give power to the arbitration to pass a decree for costs, and if the costs .are exaggerated, as the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Desearries) who is an expert in arbitration law, knows perfectly well, these costs may be reduced on a civil petition, and be brought down to adjust and exact figure. It seems to me we should retain the old .law, which is just as old as the first dispute which ever arose ini the country. The more we make exceptions in the law the more cases will crop up. Of course, if you go to the lawyers with your disputes, they will not complain.

In the province of Quebec', in a case where it is a question of damages, our judges never decide by themselves. They appoint experts who go over the locality to see for themselves what the damages are. In these cases of disputes with railways, if a judge of the Superior Court were asked to leave the bench, and go far away into the county by himself to ascertain the amount of damage on a certain property, he would refuse to do it.
By this law he will have only three witnesses to present the case before him. I think it is a great advantage to the owner when some one wants to take his land, that hr should be judged by his peers, by some

cne who knows the local conditions and all the advantages of which the owner will be deprived.

Under the old law there were three arbitrators, one selected by the owner of the land, one by the company, and the third by the other two. What could be more fair than this? I suppose the landowner would have to bring those witnesses out to see the land, then the judge could hold his court where he saw fit, and those witnesses would have to be,brought before the court, where they would be examined by the lawyer and so on. Every member of this House knows what that means. I think the old law was a great deal better and that it should be left to the arbitrators.

For fear that I will not be here when section 232 comes up, I would like to call the attention of the minister to what has given the solicitors a great deal of trouble. Section 232 deals with the question of appeals. It provides that where such party ini his notice of appeal claims more than $600 or objects to some easement or other thing approved by the arbitrator without his consent under section 222, appeal from the award upon any question of law or fact may be taken. That has created an enormous amount of litigation in Canada. I have always felt that there should not be an appeal on questions of fact. There was a case tnat went to the Privy Council about 1895, and the Privy Council decided that unless the arbitrators had proceeded upon some wrong principle of law they would not review the question of fact; they would allow that to stand as it left the arbitrator, but they would review the question of law. That was followed for quite a number of years and the courts took the ground that they were bound by this case. But within recent years all our courts have sought on one ground or another the right to depart from that very salutary principle" laid down in that case, and to hear argument and decide questions of fact as well as law. There was a case in Alberta within the last four or five years that went to the Supreme . Court of Canada. There wae a reversal of the finding on a number of questions of fact and the case proceeded until finally the Supreme Court confirmed the decision of the arbitrators. In my own province our courts for a long time held they had no right to review questions of fact, but in the last case' brought before the courts they upset what had been the law for the past twenty years, turned down the findings of the arbitrators and found new facts for them-

selves. This has caused a great 10 p.m. deal of litigation and trouble in Canada. I hope the minister will take the trouble to consult with the proper officials as to whether it would not be in the interest of all parties concerned if questions of fact were left out entirely and appeals were confined to questions of law.
What if they erred in the facts?

Questions of fact must be settled by some human mind or minds, and I think the ordinary arbitrator has just as good a mind as the Supreme Court when it comes to the question of fact as to how much damage the farmer has sustained by a railway going across his land. There is no one who is better able to decide those damages than the man who is on the ground and knows the conditions. I would like to see the law so changed that the Supreme Court, or any other appeal court, would have no right to review questions of fact. I entirely agree with Mr. Price in restricting appeals as much as possible. I am altogether in sympathy with subsection 3 of this clause, in which he provides that there shall be no appeals. In Ontario a man could appeal to the High Court or to the Court of Appeal. The Supreme Court decided not many years ago that as there was no appeal from the High Court to the Supreme Court, therefore, if a party decided to go direct from the appeal judge to the High Court, he tpuld go no further. But if, instead of going to the High Court, he went direct to the Court of Appeal, he could then appeal to the Supreme Court and go from that to the Privy Council. That is actually what has happened. There are a great many incongruities as to this question of appeal. There have been too many appeals in the past. I would not only like to see the provision of subsection 3 carried out, but I would like to see the right to deal with the question of fact taken away, allowing the provision as to the question of law to stand.

I do not agree with the remarks of my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell), although I have the greatest respect for his opinion on the question. I see no reason why railways, who are so fully protected in this country, should have more protection in this respect than any other organization or any other citizen. The appeal is a great safeguard, and I believe in the clause as it stands.
It is the railway company that always exercises the right of appeal. If you examine the reports, where you will find one appeal by a farmer you will find a hundred by the railway company.
Not necessarily, both parties may feel ^aggrieved by the award of the arbitrators.	[DOT]

I am asking the nlinister to allow this clause to stand, and to consider a real question that should be decided by the minister rather than by anybody else; that is the taking away of the appeal on questions pf fact. For a great many years after the decision of the Privy Council, the courts refused to interfere with findings of fact, but within the last four or five years they have entirely thrown that to the winds and now every court in Canada is reviewing questions of fact as well, as of law.

Yes. This is an added provision that the railway' men requested.
On section 287-Orders and regulations of Board:

In the 8th and 9th lines the committee struck out the words " and may in any case limit the rate of speed of trains and locomotives as it deems proper." At the end of paragraph (g) the words " all persons travelling upon His Majesty's services " are added. Paragraph (h) is entirely new; it says:
With respect to the length of sections required to be kept in repair by employees of the company, and with respecf to the number of employees required for each section so as to ensure safety to the public.
A portion of paragraph (i) is new. After the word " trains " the following words are added " with a view to the safety of the public and of employees." (j) Is entirely new:
Limiting or regulating the hours of duty of any employees or class or classes of employees, with a view to safety.

In the other sections
you say " with a view to the safety of the public and employees " while here you only say " with a view to safety." The obvious intention of this is that no one should be overworked so that the safety of the employees and of the public shall not be endangered. We do not say that in this paragraph, we just use the word "safety." Would it be worth while to add "safety of the public and employees "?

Do you not think that the wording of the first part of paragraph (j) would indicate the meaning?
Limiting or regulating the hours of duty of any employees or class or classes of employees, with a view to safety.
Safety of whom?
Of these employees.

The purpose of paragraph (j) is to limit the number of hours

of duty with a view to the safety of the public and of the employees. If you overwork an employee you endanger the life of the employee just as much as you do that of the public. To be uniform why not say "the safety of the puiblic and of employees " in this case just as well as in the others?
There is no objection.
You think it does not mean that now?

No more than in the
other clauses, and if we make a distinction in this one, some hair-splitting lawyer m.ay say that if it was intended to protect the safety of the employees and the public we would have said so as we did in the other clauses. I would move that in paragraph (j) the words "to the public and to employees " be added after the word " safety " in the third line.

This clause deals quite
effectively with the protection of the public and of employees against accident, and there is some reference to the health of employees but I see nothing to protect the health and comfort of the public. With the advance of sanitation in the last fifteen or twenty years, the railways should be compelled by this Act to keep up-to-date in that respect. In many of our best trains the sanitation is all that could be desired, but on some of the local trains on the branch lines the lavatories are unfit for human being to occupy. This is a matter of sufficient importance to have a clause inserted giving the Board the power to compel the railway companies to keep all portions of their cars up-to-date, thoroughly clean, and pure.

I think the Railway
Board have power to deal with that now by regulation.

Is it especially referred
to in the Act? I think it is of sufficient importance to have it specially mentioned in the powers of the Railway 'Commission. In that way it could be more effectively dealt with.

I desire to move an
amendment to section 287 obliging railway companies operating passenger trains in Quebec to have on those trains only employees who understand both languages. I have seen rows and disputes of all kinds, and have sometimes seen passengers ejected from trains because they were not understood by the train -men; and I have seen others unable to make themselves, understood by ticket agents, so that they had to

call in interpreters. I think it would be well to give authority to the commission to oblige such companies to have on their passenger trains only men understanding both languages. This would work favourably for those speaking either language and it would be a great improvement in the operation of the railways in Quebec. Section 302 compels the companies to have their circulars and everything printed in both languages and it seems to me a great anomaly to have the men who are supposed to see to the observance of these circulars, laws or rules, unable .to make the passengers understand them. There is no railway company in Quebec that cannot afford to do this among their personnel.

This clause is of vast importance to the railway men, that is the men who are operating the trains. This clause has been carefully drafted to meet their views. They did not express a desire for such a provision.
We could add that to section 302. This would be binding on the company only.
Have the railway employees ever suggested anything of the kind?
It is not the employees who complain, but the passengers.
Possibly when we come to 'section 303 we could investigate it further.

Would it not be better to confer that power upon the Railway Commission? Trains made up in a foreign country, the United States for instance, might come through a portion of the province of Quebec and take on a new crew at a divisional point. Common sense should regulate all such matters. The commission could be empowered to make such regulations as they might deem wise.

Section agreed to.
On section 289-Payment of wages:
This is an important amendment. The railway men are very anxious that this section should pass.
What became of the Senate Bill dealing with this matter?
It was withdrawn, owing to the fact that this Bill was dealing with the matters dealt with in their Bill.
Will this apply to Government railways?
Yes.

This will surely increase the expense of the managing department. If this provision is adopted the railway companies will have to pay out more money each month. I can understand that employees who receive small wages should be paid fortnightly^ but I do not think that those who get big salaries should be paid oftener than once a month.
I move that the words " On and after January 1, 1918 " be inserted at the beginning of this section.

Amendment agreed to, and section as amended agreed to.
On section 291-Penalty may be prescribed:

This section was fully discussed in the committee. At one time it was decided to strike out certain portions of it, but after discussing the matter at some length the committee decided to leave the section as it was.

Section agreed to.
